title: MPSNet Interviews Head Instructor Lieutenant Colonel Gender
author: MPSNet
excerpt: MPSNet sat down with Lieutenant Colonel gendermaleehrh, Head Instructor of the Military Police School, to talk about the Middle Command, HICOM, and what it takes to join MPS.

body.text: MPSNet, the news channel of the Military Police School, recently interviewed Lieutenant Colonel gendermaleehrh, Head Instructor and member of the Middle Command. The conversation was led by MPSNet reporter 65VI9 and covered the Lieutenant Colonel's role, the daily work of MIDCOM, the current state of the school, and a message for Marines who are thinking about joining.
The Role of a Middle Command Officer
The interview opened with the most basic question: what does a Middle Command officer actually do? The answer centered on preparing new Marines for the life of a Military Police Officer.

body.q: What is your job as a Middle Command officer?
body.a: My job as a Middle Command officer is to help new Marines prepare for the life of a Military Police Officer and its duties. I also help bring values such as discipline and leadership into the Marines, so they are ready for future leadership positions.

body.text: I also help bring values such as discipline and leadership into the Marines, so they are ready for future leadership positions.

For the Head Instructor, the job goes beyond teaching procedure. The goal is to build Marines who can step into leadership roles later on, which is why discipline and leadership sit at the center of the work.

body.q: What does a typical day look like for you as a MIDCOM officer?
body.a: My daily duties as a MIDCOM officer include logging the activity of LOWCOM members and mentoring them through their journey in MPS. I also report to HICOM on any issues that come up during our duties.

body.text: The Lieutenant Colonel described MIDCOM as the middle link of the school: tracking and mentoring the Lower Command on one side, and keeping High Command informed on the other.
On High Command and the State of MPS

body.q: What do you think about the High Command of the Military Police School?
body.a: I think they are doing a great job overseeing and mentoring LOWCOM and MIDCOM members. They also step in and take over situations that LOWCOM and MIDCOM members cannot handle on their own, which keeps operations running smoothly.

body.q: What do you think about the current status of the Military Police School?
body.a: I think it is improving every day in activity. We are hosting more and more phases and tryouts, which gives more Marines the chance to show what MP is about.

body.text: It is improving every day in activity. We are hosting more and more phases and tryouts.

The Head Instructor credited HICOM for stepping in when situations are beyond the Lower and Middle Command, and pointed to the growing number of phases and tryouts as proof that activity at the school is on the rise.

body.q: Is MPS a good division for Marine personnel to join?
body.a: I think it is a good division for Marines who want to join their first division, or who want to improve their instructing and leadership skills in the USMC. It lets them build experience for future opportunities.

body.q: Do you have any words for Marine personnel who want to join MPS?
body.a: If you would like to join MPS, you should be physically and mentally prepared to handle new recruits by teaching them the core values of being a Marine, as well as the duties of an MP.

body.text: The Lieutenant Colonel pointed out two kinds of Marine who stand to gain the most from MPS: those looking for a first division, and those who want to sharpen their instructing and leadership skills. Either way, the advice to applicants was clear: be ready, both physically and mentally, to teach recruits the core values of a Marine and the duties of an MP.
MPSNet thanks Lieutenant Colonel gendermaleehrh for taking the time to speak with us.
